title: Monorepo Build Order & Affected Packages

interviewer.approach: Kahn's algorithm with a min-heap. Build adjacency from dependency to dependents (edge b -> a for [a, b]), deduplicating repeated pairs (or counting them consistently in both the in-degree and the decrement). Push every package with in-degree 0 into a min-heap; repeatedly pop the smallest, append it, and decrement its dependents, pushing any that reach 0. If the output is shorter than the package count there is a cycle: return []. O((V + E) log V) time, O(V + E) space. DFS post-order also finds a valid order and detects cycles (three colours), but doesn't give the lexicographic tie-breaking without extra work, so expect the heap version once the candidate reads the determinism requirement.
hints: Which packages can you build first? What makes a package ready later on?
Track how many unbuilt dependencies each package still has. When does that number change?
Several packages can be ready at once and you need the smallest name each time. What structure gives you the minimum efficiently as items are added?
If you can't build everything, what does that tell you about the graph?
pitfalls: Reversing the edge direction, which produces dependents before their dependencies.
Sorting the initially ready packages once and then using a plain queue, so later ties aren't broken alphabetically.
Counting a duplicated pair twice in the in-degree but decrementing once (or vice versa), so a package never becomes ready.
Missing cycle detection, or detecting only self-loops, or returning a partial order when a cycle exists.
Repeatedly scanning all packages for a ready one: O(V^2), which is slow at 10^4 packages.
Recursive DFS that overflows the stack on a 1,000-package chain in some languages.

parts.title: Affected packages for a pull request

interviewer.approach: Run part 1 to get the order (and detect cycles). Start a BFS or iterative DFS from the known changed packages over the dependency -> dependents edges, marking every reachable package. Return the part 1 order filtered to the marked set. O((V + E) log V) for the order plus O(V + E) for the traversal. An alternative is one pass over the topological order propagating an 'affected' flag from dependencies, which is elegant but only works because the order is topological.
hints: If utils changes, which packages could break? Which direction do you need to walk the dependency edges?
Can you reuse the graph and the order from part 1?
Mark everything reachable from the changed packages, then filter part 1's output.
pitfalls: Walking the edges the wrong way, returning the changed package's dependencies instead of its dependents.
Returning affected packages in discovery (BFS) order instead of build order.
Not ignoring unknown changed names, which crashes on a lookup or adds a phantom package.
Visiting a diamond's top twice and listing it twice.
Recomputing reachability from scratch for every changed package: O(changed × (V + E)).

followUps: What are the time and space complexities of each part? What changes if there are 10^6 packages and the graph doesn't fit in memory on the CI runner?
Your build order is serial. How would you schedule the builds on 8 parallel workers to minimise total build time if you knew each package's build duration?
When the graph has a cycle, returning an empty list isn't helpful to the developer. How would you report the cycle (or all of them) in a useful way?
How do you decide which packages a PR 'changed' in the first place? What about changes to a root config file, a lockfile, or a test fixture shared across packages?
The affected set for a change to a core library is almost the whole repo. How would remote caching, test sharding or a merge queue keep CI fast anyway?

interviewer.approach: A graph problem framed around monorepo tooling (Nx, Turborepo, Bazel). Part 1 is topological sort with deterministic tie-breaking and cycle detection; part 2 is reverse reachability filtered through part 1's order. Expect part 1 in about 25 minutes. Candidates who have run a monorepo should naturally discuss affected-graph computation, caching, and what counts as a change in the follow-ups; probe for that depth.

dimensions.name: Checking the AI's edge direction, tie-breaking and cycle handling
dimensions.signals: Verified which way the AI's edges point (dependency before dependent) and that it uses a min-heap rather than a sorted-once queue. Tested duplicate pairs, self-dependencies and a cycle in one component. In part 2, confirmed the AI walks dependents (not dependencies), ignores unknown names, and returns build order rather than BFS order.

levels.1: Accepted AI code with reversed edges, non-deterministic ties or no cycle detection.
levels.2: Fixed direction or tie-breaking bugs only after failing tests.
levels.3: Built small graphs (diamond, duplicate edge, cycle) to test the AI's code before trusting it.
levels.4: Told the AI the exact edge convention and determinism rule up front, reviewed its in-degree bookkeeping, and explained why a sorted-once queue is wrong.

watchFor: Reversed edges: building a package before the packages it depends on.
Sorting the initial ready set and then using a FIFO queue, so ties after the first step aren't alphabetical.
Duplicate dependency pairs counted twice in the in-degree but decremented once.
Recursive DFS without cycle detection, or one that overflows the stack on the long-chain hidden test.
Part 2: returning dependencies of the changed package instead of dependents, or BFS discovery order instead of build order.
